prompt.context: Due to the recent bankruptcy of a major airline, the aviation authority of Brazil recently opened an auction for landing and takeoff slots in one of the country's biggest airports. A slot is the right to land and depart from an airport during a given time period. Green Airlines, a small, regional airline operating in the North part of the country, was offered 10 slots for the total price of $100M. If Green accepts to buy the slots, it will have to operate them for at least 5 years.
prompt.question: The owner and CEO of Green Airlines has approached your firm looking for advice on whether they should buy the slots or not.

clarifying_info.q: What is an airport slot exactly?
clarifying_info.a: An airport slot is a permission granted by the owner of an airport, which allows the grantee to schedule a landing or departure at that airport during a specific time period.

clarifying_info.q: Does Green Airlines currently operate in this airport?
clarifying_info.a: No, Green Airlines currently does not operate in the airport that is being discussed.

clarifying_info.q: Does Green Airlines fly international flights?
clarifying_info.a: Green Airlines currently only flies regional flights and has no plans to include international flights in its offerings.

clarifying_info.q: Does Green Airlines have planes to operate the slots?
clarifying_info.a: No, Green Airlines does not currently have the necessary planes to operate the slots. Management will need to lease 5 airplanes to operate the 10 slots.
The $100M is a one-off payment, due before operations start.

clarifying_info.q: What is the main objective of the CEO?
clarifying_info.a: The main objective of the owner/CEO is financial gain.

clarifying_info.q: Can the slots be sold after purchase?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, Green Airlines can sell the slots, but only after five years of operation.

clarifying_info.q: What happens if Green Airlines does not buy the slots?
clarifying_info.a: If Green Airlines does not buy the slots, they will be sold to another airline.

exhibits.title: Competitive Landscape and Airline Comparison
exhibits.shows: A map of Brazil showing the geographic location of each airline's main hub, and a table comparing four airlines (Airlines A, Airlines B, Airlines C, and Green Airlines) on key operational metrics.

framework: Market: Demand trends at target airport; traveler profile (business vs. leisure); financial health of industry vs. one-off bankruptcy
Competition: Number of operators at airport; slot concentration; presence of low-cost carriers; competitor pricing
Revenues & Costs: Passengers per slot (plane size × load factor × flights/day); ticket price; fixed costs (leasing, salaries, insurance/fees); variable costs (fuel, other)
Internal Capabilities: Operational capabilities (planes, overhead, sales system, suppliers); strategic fit with big-airport operations; financial capacity to fund $100M purchase
Risks & Alternatives: Cultural/operational challenges of new region; alternative regions; possibility to buy and resell slots to larger airlines

questions.prompt: Estimate the monthly revenue if Green Airlines operates the 10 slots.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify key revenue drivers: number of planes, flights per plane per month, seats per plane, load factor, and ticket price. Strong candidates will reference Exhibit 1 to benchmark assumptions against market data.

math.setup: Revenue per month = # planes × flights/plane/month × seats/plane × load factor × ticket price

questions.prompt: Estimate the monthly costs of operating the 10 slots and the expected annual profit.
questions.guidance: Candidate should enumerate major airline cost categories: fuel, other variable costs, salaries, maintenance & leasing, insurance/fees. After tallying all costs, candidate should compare to revenue and compute expected profit including initial setup investment.

math.setup: Monthly costs = fuel + other variable costs + salaries + maintenance & leasing + insurance/fees/others
math.answer: Year 1: -$5M; Years 2–5: $0 per year. Operating break-even, net loss after setup cost.

questions.prompt: Given operational profit is zero, what alternatives should Green Airlines consider? What is the value of these slots to a larger airline such as Airlines A or Airlines C?
questions.guidance: Candidate should first brainstorm ways to improve operational metrics (revenue increases or cost reductions), then pivot to the key insight: slots may be worth far more to larger airlines that operate bigger planes. Candidate should calculate the revenue for a large airline (300-seat planes) and then value the slots as a perpetuity.

math.setup: Step 1 – Revenue for big airline: same formula but with 300-seat planes. Step 2 – Monthly profit for big airline. Step 3 – Slot valuation as perpetuity: Value = Annual profit / Discount rate
steps: Big airline monthly cost = $10M/month (same cost structure)
math.answer: Slots are worth approximately $240M to a large airline. Green Airlines can buy for $100M, operate at breakeven for 5 years, and sell for a price between $105M (just above cost) and $240M (full value), netting up to ~$135M profit.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the potential ways for Green Airlines to improve the operational result of the 10 slots?

categories.name: Revenue Improvements
ideas: Increase ticket price on certain routes
Add non-ticket revenues (baggage fees, seat upgrades, onboard sales)
Offer travel packages bundled with hotels/tours
Add shuttle service connections to other cities
Partner with travel agencies for volume bookings

categories.name: Cost Reductions
ideas: Use bigger planes to spread fixed costs over more seats
Negotiate better lease terms for aircraft
Eliminate or charge for inflight food
Renegotiate with fuel suppliers or hedge fuel costs
Reduce overhead by sharing infrastructure with partners

categories.name: Alternative Uses of Slots
ideas: Sell slots immediately to Airlines A or C after 5-year mandatory operation period
Sub-lease or partner with a larger airline to operate the slots on Green's behalf
Use slots as leverage to negotiate a merger or acquisition premium
Hold slots as strategic asset and sell when market conditions improve

recommendation: Green Airlines should buy the 10 slots for $100M
Operate the slots for the mandatory 5 years at approximately breakeven (net -$5M in Year 1, $0 thereafter)
After 5 years, sell the slots to a major airline (Airlines A or Airlines C) for a price between $105M and $240M
The expected profit on the transaction is approximately $135M, far exceeding the initial investment
risks: Operational risk: Green Airlines lacks experience in large hub airports; learning curve may increase costs above projections
Financial risk: $100M upfront payment is significant relative to Green Airlines' current size (6 planes); requires external financing
Market risk: Slot values could decline if aviation market weakens or larger airlines lose interest
Execution risk: Inability to find a buyer at expected price after 5 years of mandatory operation
Regulatory risk: Rules around slot sales could change over the 5-year period
next_steps: Conduct detailed financial modeling with financing scenarios for the $100M upfront payment
Initiate informal discussions with Airlines A and Airlines C to gauge interest and validate slot valuation
Develop an operational plan for the 5-year mandatory operation period to minimize cash burn
Engage legal counsel to review slot auction terms and resale conditions
Assess financing options: equity raise, bank debt, or strategic partner co-investment
